topics.title: Covalent bonding and the versatile carbon

learn.hook: Carbon is the ultimate team player — it shares instead of grabbing or giving away electrons!
points: Carbon (atomic number 6, configuration 2, 4) has 4 valence electrons. Gaining 4 (C⁴⁻) or losing 4 (C⁴⁺) needs too much energy, so carbon shares electrons.
A covalent bond forms when atoms share a pair of electrons. H₂ has a single bond, O₂ a double bond (2 shared pairs) and N₂ a triple bond (3 shared pairs).
Covalent compounds have weak forces between molecules, so they usually have low melting and boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity.
Tetravalency (valency 4) and catenation (bonding with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branches and rings) let carbon form a huge number of compounds. Its small size makes its bonds strong.

Allotropes of carbon: diamond (each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D network, hardest natural substance), graphite (each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers, slippery and conducts electricity) and fullerenes like C₆₀, shaped like a football.

example.q: Think it through: how many electrons are shared in a molecule of nitrogen, N₂?
steps: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons (2, 5) and needs 3 more for an octet.
Each nitrogen atom contributes 3 electrons to sharing.
That makes 3 shared pairs — a triple bond.
3 pairs × 2 electrons = 6 electrons.
example.answer: 6 electrons (3 shared pairs, a triple bond)

learn.reallife: The 'lead' in your pencil is actually graphite: its layers slide off onto paper. Diamonds cut glass and are used in drilling tools because they are so hard.

games.title: Match the molecule to its bond

items: Each carbon bonded to four others
Each carbon bonded to three others
Hardest natural substance
Good conductor of electricity
Layers slide over each other
Rigid three-dimensional network
Used in pencils and as a lubricant
Used in cutting and drilling tools

quiz.q: Why does carbon form covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds?
options: It has no electrons in its outer shell
Gaining or losing 4 electrons needs too much energy, so it shares them
quiz.explain: With 4 valence electrons, forming C⁴⁻ or C⁴⁺ is very difficult, so carbon reaches a stable octet by sharing.
steps: Carbon (2, 4) has 4 valence electrons.
Gaining 4 (C⁴⁻) or losing 4 (C⁴⁺) needs too much energy.
So carbon reaches a stable octet by sharing electrons, forming covalent bonds.
Answer: Gaining or losing 4 electrons needs too much energy, so it shares them
quiz.mistake: Thinks carbon readily forms ions

quiz.q: How many covalent bonds does one carbon atom form in methane (CH₄)?
quiz.explain: Carbon is tetravalent: it shares one electron pair with each of the 4 hydrogen atoms.
steps: Carbon is tetravalent: it forms 4 bonds.
In CH₄ it shares one electron pair with each of the 4 hydrogen atoms.
So it forms 4 covalent bonds.
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Counts only some of the hydrogens

quiz.q: Which molecule contains a double bond?
quiz.explain: Each oxygen (2, 6) needs 2 electrons, so two pairs are shared — a double bond. N₂ has a triple bond.
steps: Oxygen (2, 6) needs 2 more electrons.
Two oxygen atoms share 2 pairs → a double bond.
H₂ and Cl₂ have single bonds; N₂ has a triple bond.
So O₂ has a double bond.
Answer: O₂
quiz.mistake: Confuses oxygen's double bond with nitrogen's triple bond

quiz.q: Covalent compounds generally have —
options: High melting points and conduct electricity
Low melting points and are poor conductors of electricity
High melting points and are brittle ionic crystals
quiz.explain: Forces between covalent molecules are weak, and no ions are formed, so melting points are low and electricity is not conducted.
steps: Forces between covalent molecules are weak → low melting and boiling points.
Covalent compounds form no ions → poor conductors of electricity.
So they have low melting points and are poor conductors of electricity.
Answer: Low melting points and are poor conductors of electricity
quiz.mistake: Mixes up covalent and ionic properties

quiz.q: The property of carbon atoms to link with other carbon atoms to form long chains is called —
quiz.explain: Catenation is self-linking to form chains, branches and rings. Tetravalency means valency 4.
steps: Catenation = carbon linking with other carbon atoms to form chains, branches and rings.
Tetravalency means valency 4; allotropy means different forms of the element.
So the property is catenation.
Answer: Catenation
quiz.mistake: Swaps catenation and tetravalency

quiz.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
options: Graphite has free electrons because each carbon bonds to only three others
Diamond is made of a different element
quiz.explain: In graphite each carbon uses three electrons for bonding with neighbours, leaving electrons free to move. In diamond all four are used.
steps: In graphite each carbon bonds to only 3 others.
That leaves electrons free to move, so graphite conducts.
In diamond all 4 electrons are used in bonding, so it does not conduct.
So graphite has free electrons because each carbon bonds to only three others.
Answer: Graphite has free electrons because each carbon bonds to only three others
quiz.mistake: Thinks allotropes are different elements

quiz.q: C₆₀, shaped like a football, belongs to which group of carbon allotropes?
quiz.explain: C₆₀ is a fullerene, named after the architect Buckminster Fuller whose domes it resembles.
steps: Carbon allotropes: diamond, graphite and fullerenes.
C₆₀ is shaped like a football and is a fullerene.
So it belongs to the fullerenes.
Answer: Fullerenes
quiz.mistake: Thinks carbon has only two allotropes

quiz.q: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in a molecule of N₂?
quiz.explain: Nitrogen (2, 5) needs 3 electrons, so the two atoms share 3 pairs — a triple bond.
steps: Nitrogen (2, 5) needs 3 more electrons.
Two nitrogen atoms share 3 pairs → a triple bond.
So there are 3 shared pairs (6 electrons).
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Counts electrons instead of pairs, or uses oxygen's double bond

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does carbon share electrons instead of giving them away like sodium? What is a covalent bond?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Carbon has four valence electrons and shares them in pairs — that's a covalent bond!
teach.nudge: Good! But how many electrons does carbon have in its outer shell, and why doesn't it just lose them?

revise.summary: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and shares them to form covalent bonds. Its tetravalency and catenation let it form a huge number of compounds; its allotropes include diamond, graphite and fullerenes.
focus: Draw single, double and triple bonds (H₂, O₂, N₂, CH₄)
Explain why covalent compounds have low melting points and do not conduct
Compare diamond, graphite and fullerene structures and properties
remember: Tetravalency = valency 4; catenation = carbon linking to carbon in chains, branches and rings
Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others; graphite: each C bonded to 3 others, conducts electricity
N₂ has a triple bond (3 shared pairs = 6 electrons)
traps: Carbon does not form C⁴⁺ or C⁴⁻ ions easily; it shares electrons
Don't mix up catenation and tetravalency
Graphite conducts but diamond does not, though both are pure carbon

topics.title: Hydrocarbons, homologous series and functional groups

learn.hook: Add one CH₂ at a time and you climb a ladder of compounds — methane, ethane, propane, butane!
points: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Saturated ones (alkanes, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) have only single bonds; unsaturated ones have a double bond (alkenes, CₙH₂ₙ) or a triple bond (alkynes, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
Carbon chains can be straight, branched or ring-shaped (cyclohexane C₆H₁₂, benzene C₆H₆). Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are isomers — butane C₄H₁₀ has two.
A homologous series is a family with the same functional group in which each member differs from the next by –CH₂– (14 u). Chemical properties are similar; physical properties change gradually.
Functional groups give compounds their properties: halo (–Cl, –Br), alcohol (–OH), aldehyde (–CHO), ketone (>C=O) and carboxylic acid (–COOH).
Naming: the stem tells the number of carbons (meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4) and the ending or prefix tells the group: propanol, propanal, propanone, propanoic acid, chloropropane, propene.

steps: Count carbons: 3, so the stem is 'propan-'.
The functional group is –OH, an alcohol, so the ending is '-ol'.
Put them together.

learn.reallife: The LPG cylinder in your kitchen contains butane and propane, and CNG used in autos and buses is mainly methane — both members of the alkane family.

games.title: Match the compound to its functional group
Climb the alkane ladder
items: Methane, CH₄
Ethane, C₂H₆
Propane, C₃H₈
Butane, C₄H₁₀
Pentane, C₅H₁₂

quiz.q: What is the molecular formula of propane?
quiz.explain: Propane is an alkane with 3 carbons: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ gives C₃H₈.
steps: Propane is an alkane; alkanes follow CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
So propane is C₃H₈.
Answer: C₃H₈
quiz.mistake: Uses the alkene formula CₙH₂ₙ

quiz.q: Which of these is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
quiz.explain: Ethene (C₂H₄) has a carbon–carbon double bond, so it is unsaturated.
steps: Unsaturated hydrocarbons have a double or triple bond.
Ethene (C₂H₄) has a C=C double bond.
Ethane, methane and butane have only single bonds (saturated).
So ethene is unsaturated.
Answer: Ethene
quiz.mistake: Thinks the '-ane' and '-ene' endings mean the same

quiz.q: By how many mass units (u) do two successive members of a homologous series differ?
quiz.explain: They differ by –CH₂–: 12 + 2 × 1 = 14 u.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the carbon (12) or only the hydrogens (2)
steps: Difference is CH₂
Answer: 14

quiz.q: Butane and isobutane both have the formula C₄H₁₀ but different structures. They are called —
quiz.explain: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements.
steps: Butane and isobutane have the same molecular formula, C₄H₁₀.
Their structures are different.
Same formula, different structure = isomers.
So they are isomers.
Answer: Isomers
quiz.mistake: Confuses isomers with allotropes (forms of an element)

quiz.q: What is the correct name of CH₃COCH₃?
quiz.explain: It has 3 carbons with a ketone group in the middle, so it is propanone (commonly acetone).
steps: CH₃COCH₃ has 3 carbons → stem 'prop'.
The C=O is in the middle of the chain → ketone → ending '-one'.
So the name is propanone.
Answer: Propanone
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the aldehyde and ketone endings

quiz.q: Which functional group is present in ethanoic acid?
quiz.explain: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) has the carboxylic acid group, –COOH.
steps: Ethanoic acid is CH₃COOH.
It contains the carboxylic acid group.
That group is –COOH.
Answer: –COOH
quiz.mistake: Thinks the –OH inside –COOH makes it an alcohol

quiz.q: What is the general formula of alkynes?
quiz.explain: Alkynes have one triple bond and follow CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, e.g. ethyne C₂H₂.
steps: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
Check: ethyne, n = 2 → H = 2 × 2 − 2 = 2 → C₂H₂ ✓.
So alkynes follow CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
Answer: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the alkene and alkyne formulae

quiz.q: Which statement about a homologous series is correct?
options: Members show similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties
All members have the same molecular formula
All members have the same boiling point
quiz.explain: Same functional group gives similar chemistry; growing chain length makes melting and boiling points rise gradually.
steps: Members of a homologous series have the same functional group → similar chemical properties.
Each member differs by –CH₂–, so physical properties change gradually.
They do not share one molecular formula or one boiling point.
So: similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
Answer: Members show similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties
quiz.mistake: Confuses a homologous series with isomers

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'Methane, ethane, propane... why do these names sound like a family? And what makes ethanol different from ethane?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Each member adds a CH₂, and the –OH functional group turns ethane into ethanol!
teach.nudge: Nice! Now tell me what is added each time we go to the next member.

revise.summary: Hydrocarbons can be saturated (alkanes) or unsaturated (alkenes, alkynes) and can form chains, branches or rings. Compounds are grouped into homologous series and named by carbon count plus functional group.
focus: Use the general formulae of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
Name compounds with halo, alcohol, aldehyde, ketone and carboxylic acid groups
remember: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; alkenes CₙH₂ₙ; alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
Successive members of a homologous series differ by –CH₂– (14 u)
Groups: –OH alcohol, –CHO aldehyde, >C=O ketone, –COOH carboxylic acid
traps: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures; they are not allotropes
Propanal (–CHO) and propanone (>C=O) are different compounds
Members of a series do not have the same boiling point; it changes gradually

topics.title: Chemical properties, ethanol and ethanoic acid

learn.hook: The same carbon compounds that burn in a gas stove can also turn into the sour vinegar in your pickle jar!
points: Combustion: carbon compounds burn in oxygen to give CO₂, water, heat and light. Saturated hydrocarbons generally burn with a clean flame; unsaturated ones give a yellow, sooty flame.
Oxidation: alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate (oxidising agents) convert ethanol into ethanoic acid.

Addition: unsaturated compounds add hydrogen in the presence of a nickel or palladium catalyst — this hydrogenation turns vegetable oils into solid fats. Substitution: in sunlight, chlorine replaces hydrogen in methane: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
Ethanol (C₂H₅OH): reacts with sodium to give sodium ethoxide and hydrogen; heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K it loses water to form ethene.

Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH): a weak acid; 5–8% solution in water is vinegar; pure acid can freeze in cold weather (glacial acetic acid). With ethanol and an acid catalyst it forms a sweet-smelling ester (esterification); esters with NaOH give back alcohol and a salt (saponification). It reacts with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give CO₂.

example.q: Think it through: the bottom of Ma's cooking vessel is getting black. What is wrong with the burner?
steps: Black soot appears when fuel burns incompletely.
Incomplete combustion happens when there is not enough air (oxygen).
So the air holes of the burner are probably blocked.
example.answer: The air holes are blocked, so the fuel is not getting enough oxygen; cleaning them gives a clean blue flame.

learn.reallife: Pickles and chutneys use vinegar (dilute ethanoic acid) as a preservative, and many fruity smells in sweets and perfumes come from esters.

quiz.q: Which hydrocarbon is most likely to burn with a yellow, sooty flame?
quiz.explain: Ethyne is unsaturated (triple bond); unsaturated hydrocarbons give a yellow flame with lots of black smoke.
steps: Saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean flame.
Unsaturated ones give a yellow, sooty flame.
Ethyne has a triple bond (unsaturated); methane, ethane and propane are saturated.
So ethyne burns with a yellow, sooty flame.
Answer: Ethyne
quiz.mistake: Does not link sooty flames with unsaturation

quiz.q: Alkaline potassium permanganate converts ethanol into —
quiz.explain: KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent; it oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid.
steps: Alkaline KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent.
It oxidises ethanol (C₂H₅OH) to ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH).
So the product is ethanoic acid.
Answer: Ethanoic acid
quiz.mistake: Confuses oxidation with dehydration

quiz.q: Hydrogenation of vegetable oil is an example of —
quiz.explain: Hydrogen adds across the double bonds of unsaturated oils, using a nickel catalyst.
steps: In hydrogenation, hydrogen adds across the double bonds of an unsaturated oil (nickel catalyst).
Adding to a double bond is an addition reaction.
So it is an addition reaction.
Answer: Addition reaction
quiz.mistake: Thinks hydrogen replaces atoms instead of adding

quiz.q: What forms when ethanol is heated at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid?
quiz.explain: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes water from ethanol (dehydration), giving ethene.
steps: Hot concentrated H₂SO₄ removes water from ethanol (dehydration).
C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O at 443 K.
So ethene forms.
Answer: Ethene
quiz.mistake: Mixes up dehydration with oxidation

quiz.q: Why is pure ethanoic acid called glacial acetic acid?
options: It freezes into ice-like crystals in cold weather
It is very cold to touch
quiz.explain: Its melting point is 290 K (about 17 °C), so it often freezes in winter, looking like a glacier.
steps: Pure ethanoic acid melts at 290 K (about 17 °C).
So in cold weather it freezes into ice-like crystals.
That is why it is called glacial acetic acid.
Answer: It freezes into ice-like crystals in cold weather
quiz.mistake: Takes the name literally

quiz.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst. The product is —
quiz.explain: This is esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester ethyl ethanoate smells sweet.
steps: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (acid catalyst).
This is esterification.
The product, ethyl ethanoate, is a sweet-smelling ester.
Answer: An ester
quiz.mistake: Confuses esterification with saponification

quiz.q: In sunlight, methane and chlorine react to form chloromethane and HCl. This is a —
quiz.explain: A chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom, so it is substitution.
steps: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in sunlight.
A chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom.
Replacing one atom by another is a substitution reaction.
Answer: Substitution reaction
quiz.mistake: Thinks any reaction with chlorine is addition

quiz.q: What gas is evolved when ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate?
quiz.explain: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. CO₂ turns lime water milky.
steps: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
The gas given off turns lime water milky.
So the gas is carbon dioxide.
Answer: Carbon dioxide
quiz.mistake: Thinks acids always give hydrogen

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does ethanol turn into the vinegar in my achaar? And what is an ester?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Oxidise ethanol and you get ethanoic acid; mix the two and you get a sweet-smelling ester!
teach.nudge: Close! What kind of reaction turns ethanol into ethanoic acid?

revise.summary: Carbon compounds undergo combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are two important compounds with their own typical reactions, such as esterification.
focus: Tell combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions apart
Know the reactions of ethanol (with sodium, with hot conc. H₂SO₄)
Know the reactions of ethanoic acid (esterification, with carbonates) and saponification
remember: Alkaline KMnO₄ or acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid
Hydrogenation of oils uses a nickel or palladium catalyst (addition)
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in sunlight (substitution)
Ethanol + hot conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K → ethene; ethanoic acid + ethanol → ester
traps: Unsaturated hydrocarbons, not saturated ones, give a yellow sooty flame
Glacial acetic acid is pure ethanoic acid that freezes in cold weather, not acid mixed with ice
Esterification makes an ester; saponification turns an ester back into alcohol and a salt

learn.hook: Soap molecules are like tiny tadpoles: one end loves water, the other loves oil — together they kidnap the dirt!
points: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. They are made by saponification of fats or oils with sodium hydroxide.
A soap molecule has an ionic (hydrophilic) end that dissolves in water and a long hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) tail that dissolves in oil.
In water, soap molecules form clusters called micelles: tails point inward around the oily dirt, ionic ends face outward into the water, so the dirt is rinsed away.
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble, sticky precipitate called scum, so more soap is wasted.

Detergents are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions. Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so they work well even in hard water; they are used in shampoos and washing powders.

example.q: Think it through: a student washes a muddy kurta with soap in tube-well water and sees a white curdy mass instead of lather. Why?
steps: The tube-well water is probably hard, containing calcium and magnesium salts.
Soap reacts with these ions to form an insoluble precipitate (scum).
Soap is used up in forming scum, so little lather forms.
A detergent would work better here.
example.answer: The water is hard; soap forms scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions instead of lathering, so a detergent should be used.

learn.reallife: When you wash greasy hands after eating samosas, soap micelles trap the oil inside them so water can carry it down the drain.

games.title: How soap cleans an oily cloth
items: Soap dissolves in water
Hydrophobic tails stick into the oily dirt
Micelles form, with oil trapped in the centre and ionic ends facing the water
Scrubbing lifts the micelles off the cloth into the water
Rinsing washes the micelles and dirt away

games.title: Soap or detergent? True or false
items: Soap forms scum in hard water.
Calcium and magnesium ions form an insoluble precipitate with soap.
Detergents work in hard water as well.
Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions.
The hydrocarbon tail of a soap molecule dissolves in water.
The tail is hydrophobic and dissolves in oil; the ionic end dissolves in water.
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts.
These salts make water hard.
Soaps are salts of short-chain carboxylic acids.
Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.
Detergents are used to make shampoos and products for washing clothes.
They clean well even in hard water.

quiz.q: Soaps are —
options: Sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids
quiz.explain: Soap is made by saponifying fats or oils with alkali, giving salts of long-chain fatty acids.
steps: Soap is made by saponifying fats or oils with an alkali.
The products are salts of long-chain fatty (carboxylic) acids.
So soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.
Answer: Sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids
quiz.mistake: Confuses soaps with detergents or esters

quiz.q: In a micelle, the hydrocarbon tails of soap molecules point —
options: Out of the water into the air only
quiz.explain: The hydrophobic tails avoid water and cluster around the oil at the centre, while the ionic heads face the water.
steps: The hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic (avoids water) and dissolves in oil.
In a micelle the tails cluster around the oily dirt at the centre.
So the tails point inward, towards the oily dirt.
Answer: Inward, towards the oily dirt
quiz.mistake: Reverses the hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends

quiz.q: Why does soap not lather well in hard water?
options: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts to form scum
Hard water contains too much sodium
quiz.explain: The insoluble precipitate (scum) uses up soap, so little lather forms.
steps: Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts.
Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble, sticky precipitate called scum.
The scum wastes soap, so little lather forms.
Answer: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts to form scum
quiz.mistake: Thinks hardness is about temperature

quiz.q: Which part of a soap molecule is hydrophilic (water-loving)?
quiz.explain: The ionic (charged) end interacts with water; the hydrocarbon chain is hydrophobic.
steps: Hydrophilic means water-loving.
The ionic (charged) end of soap interacts with water.
The long hydrocarbon chain is hydrophobic.
So the ionic end is hydrophilic.
Answer: The ionic end
quiz.mistake: Mixes up hydrophilic and hydrophobic

quiz.q: Why are detergents preferred for washing clothes in hard water?
options: Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions
They soften the water by boiling it
quiz.explain: Detergents stay effective because they do not form scum with hardness ions.
steps: Soap forms scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in hard water.
The charged ends of detergents do not form insoluble precipitates with these ions.
So detergents keep working in hard water.
Answer: Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions
quiz.mistake: Thinks detergents work by removing all salts

quiz.q: The reaction of an oil or fat with sodium hydroxide to make soap is called —
quiz.explain: Saponification means 'soap-making': esters of fatty acids react with alkali to give soap and glycerol.
steps: Oil or fat + sodium hydroxide → soap (+ glycerol).
This soap-making reaction is called saponification.
So the answer is saponification.
Answer: Saponification
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with esterification, the reverse kind of reaction

quiz.q: A sample of water gives a lot of curdy white precipitate and little lather with soap. The water is —
quiz.explain: Curdy precipitate (scum) is a sign of calcium and magnesium salts — hard water.
steps: Curdy white precipitate with soap = scum.
Scum forms with calcium and magnesium salts.
Water containing these salts is hard water.
Answer: Hard water
quiz.mistake: Thinks precipitate shows soft water

quiz.q: Why can't plain water alone wash oily dirt off a plate?
options: Oil does not dissolve in water, and without soap no micelles form to carry it
quiz.explain: Oil and water do not mix. Soap is needed to form micelles that hold oil in water as an emulsion.
steps: Oil does not dissolve in water, so water alone cannot lift it.
Soap forms micelles that hold oil inside and carry it into the water.
Without soap no micelles form.
So plain water cannot wash oily dirt.
Answer: Oil does not dissolve in water, and without soap no micelles form to carry it
quiz.mistake: Believes water alone can lift grease

teach.ask: Gappu has oily feathers: 'How does soap pull oil off me when water can't? And why doesn't it foam in our tube-well water?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Tails grab oil, heads hold water, micelles carry dirt away — and hard water makes scum!
teach.nudge: Good! Now explain which end of the soap holds the oil and which end faces water.

revise.summary: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Their molecules form micelles that trap oily dirt. Soap forms scum in hard water, but detergents work well in hard water.
focus: Explain the hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends of a soap molecule
Describe how micelles remove oily dirt
Explain scum formation in hard water and why detergents are better there
remember: Soap is made by saponification of fats or oils with sodium hydroxide
In a micelle, tails point inward to the oil and ionic ends face the water
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts; soap + these salts → scum
traps: The ionic end is hydrophilic; the hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic, not the other way round
Detergents do not form scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, so they are not wasted in hard water
